steps.label: Statements
steps.body:
Three statements, and two of them are conditionals ("must" and "no insect brain").

Instinctual behavior → no reasoning, far fewer nerve cells than flexible behavior
Capable of flexible behavior → large number of neurons
Insect brain → NOT a large enough number of neurons

One more fact hides in a parenthesis: noninstinctual behavior is "also called flexible." So there are only two kinds of behavior here. Behavior that isn't flexible is instinctual.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
On Must Be True, conditionals and shared terms come first. Do any of these rules share a term?

Yes. The second and third both talk about a large number of neurons. The second says flexible behavior requires it. The third says insect brains don't have it. Take the contrapositive of the second (NOT large number of neurons → NOT capable of flexible behavior) and attach it to the third:

Insect brain → NOT large number of neurons → NOT capable of flexible behavior

And since anything that isn't flexible is instinctual, insect behavior is instinctual.

Notice what this chain can't do. A large number of neurons is a requirement for flexible behavior, not a guarantee. So we know what lacking the neurons rules out. Having them proves nothing.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Predict the end of the chain: insects can't behave flexibly, so insect behavior is instinctual.

Expect traps that read the neuron requirement backwards, treating a large brain as enough for flexible behavior, or treating a small brain as the only route to pure instinct.

notes.body: "Usually not instinctual" is a claim about how organisms with elaborate brains actually behave. The stimulus gives a requirement for flexible behavior, so it can only tell us who can't behave flexibly. An organism with plenty of neurons could still run on instinct most of the time without breaking any statement.

Run the chain from insects. No insect brain provides a sufficiently large number of neurons, and flexible behavior requires one, so no insect brain is capable of flexible behavior. The stimulus defines flexible as noninstinctual, so whatever insects do is instinctual.

"Exclusively" sounds strong, but it's earned: the requirement is missing for every insect, so there is no room for even a little flexible behavior. When a strong word shows up on Must Be True, check whether a universal rule (here, "no insect brain") backs it before crossing it off.

Larger than an insect's brain isn't the same as large enough. The stimulus only says insect brains fall short. A brain could beat an insect's and still lack the neurons. And even a brain with enough neurons isn't guaranteed flexible behavior, because the neuron count is a requirement, not a guarantee.

This reverses the rule. Capable of flexible behavior → large number of neurons says the neurons are required. D reads it as large brain → equipped for flexible behavior, treating the requirement as enough. Driving legally requires a license, but holding a license doesn't make someone a driver. D also swaps "large brain" for "large number of neurons," which the stimulus never equates.

E says purely instinctual → brain of insect size or smaller. We only know the other direction: insect → instinctual. An organism with a bigger brain that still falls short of the neuron count would also be limited to instinct, and nothing rules that out. "Only" makes a small brain a requirement for pure instinct, and the stimulus never sets that requirement.

old_steps.label: Facts
old_steps.body:
conditionals (must, no, universal noun)
Flexible —requires→ large # of neurons behavior
Insect brain → doesn't have large # of neurons Instinctual → No reasoning and behavior fewer nerve cells than flex behavior

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body:
The #1 thing we read for on MBT is conditionals. We found three of them. Do they chain together? Do they have any overlapping concepts?
Yes, two of them mention flexible behavior. Two of them mention a large # of neurons. The last two claims chain together to give us this,
Insect → not large # → not flexible brain of neurons behavior
That idea of "not flexible" behavior is the same as instinctual behavior, so we could also chain on the first claim.
Insect → not large # → not flexible → no reasoning brain of neurons behavior fewer nerve cells

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: Let's look for anything we can prove. It'll probably reward us for having assembled this chain, though not necessarily with a Head → Tail inference.

old_notes.body: Large brains make flexible behavior possible. Nothing says such organisms usually use it.
Flexible behavior needs many neurons, and no insect brain has enough. The only other kind of behavior is instinctual, so insect behavior is all instinctual.
Being larger than an insect's brain doesn't mean a brain has enough neurons for flexible behavior.
A large number of neurons is required for flexible behavior, not enough for it. A large brain isn't guaranteed to be equipped.
Insects are limited to instinct, but other organisms could be too. Nothing makes insect-sized brains the only ones.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Three rules about which authors make the book.

1. At least one of Lind, Knight, and Jones is in. ("Lind, Knight, or Jones")
2. Not all three are in.
3. K → J

Rule 3 is the one with a consequence. Pick Knight and Jones comes along. Now we have two of the three, and rule 2 says the third can't join. So:

K → J → ~L

Lind is blocked whenever Knight is in. Take the contrapositive:

L → ~K

Notice what we can't say. Knight doesn't have to be in. Lind doesn't have to be in. A book with Jones alone breaks no rule, and neither does a book with Lind alone. Rules like these limit combinations. They don't force any single author into the book.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Since nothing forces any one author in or out, expect a conditional answer: K → ~L or its contrapositive, L → ~K.

Any answer that makes a flat claim about one author, or about how many authors appear, can be tested the same way: build a legal book that breaks it. If you can, it doesn't have to be true.

notes.body:
This is the contrapositive we built. Suppose Lind is in and Knight is also in. Knight drags Jones in, and now the book has all three, which rule 2 forbids. So Lind in means Knight out.

The move to repeat: when one rule forces an item to bring a second, check whether that pair runs into a limit (here, "not all three") that blocks a third. That blocked combination is often the inference.

Only one author? Build a legal book with two: Knight and Jones. Rule 1 is met, rule 2 is met because Lind is out, and Knight brought Jones as rule 3 demands. Two authors and no broken rule, so B doesn't have to be true.
Knight can be in. A book with Knight and Jones and no Lind satisfies every rule. The rules only say that Knight's presence has consequences (Jones in, Lind out). They never exclude Knight.

Lind doesn't bring Jones. A book with Lind alone satisfies all three rules: at least one author, not all three, and rule 3 never triggers because Knight is absent. So L → J doesn't have to hold. D borrows Jones from the Knight rule and attaches it to Lind.
Lind isn't required. A book with Knight and Jones satisfies every rule without Lind, and so does a book with Jones alone. Rule 1 says at least one of the three is in, not which one.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: Given that the book can't have all three authors, if we include Knight (and thus have to include Jones), then we definitely won't be including Lind. That ends up looking like K → ~L or by contrapositive L → ~K

old_notes.body:
This follows from the 1st and 2nd statements.
K → J
K + J → ~L
∴ L → ~K

If Lind were one of the two we were picking, then Knight can't be the other one we pick (because when we pick Knight we **also** have to pick Jones!)
The textbook could contain entries by both Knight and Jones
The textbook could contain entries by both Knight and Jones.
The textbook could contain an essay by only Lind.
The textbook could contain essays by both Knight and Jones, but not Lind.

steps.label: Statements
steps.body:
Only people who are **willing to compromise** should undergo **mediation** to resolve their conflicts.

M → WC

Actual **litigation** should be pursued only when one is **sure** that one's position is **correct**.

L → SC

People whose **conflicts are based on ideology** are **unwilling to compromise**.

I → ~WC

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Three conditionals. Is there a term they share?

Willingness to compromise shows up twice. Mediation requires it (first rule), and ideological conflicts lack it (third rule). That overlap is the hinge. Flip the first rule with its contrapositive and attach it to the third:

I → ~WC
~WC → ~M

So: I → ~WC → ~M.

What about litigation? L → SC shares no term with the other two. Being sure of your position never connects to compromise or ideology, so that rule is a dead end. Any answer that bridges it to the others is inventing a link.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Predict I → ~M: people in ideological conflicts should not undergo mediation.

Then watch for two traps: answers that start from a negated trigger or a necessary condition (those trigger nothing), and answers that try to connect the litigation rule to anything else.

notes.body: A starts from people who do not undergo mediation. That negates the trigger of the first rule, so it tells us nothing. And to reach "should be sure," A has to assume these people should litigate. Nothing says that someone who skips mediation should go to court. They could drop the conflict entirely.

Not based on ideology negates the trigger of the third rule, so we learn nothing about compromise. Even if we did, no rule ever says anyone should pursue litigation. The litigation rule only gives a requirement (being sure), never a recommendation.

C connects ideology to being sure. The rules link ideology to compromise, and compromise to mediation. Being sure only appears in the litigation rule, which connects to nothing else. People in ideological conflicts could be completely sure of themselves without breaking any rule.

Being sure is the necessary side of the litigation rule, so it can't trigger anything. D also ties sureness to mediation, but sureness never touches compromise. Someone sure of their position and willing to compromise could undergo mediation, and no rule says otherwise.

Chain the third rule into the contrapositive of the first. I → ~WC, and ~WC → ~M. So I → ~M: people whose conflicts are based on ideology are not people who should undergo mediation. That's E.

The move: find the term two rules share (willingness to compromise), line the rules up so the shared term sits in the middle, flipping one with its contrapositive if needed, and read off the two ends.

old_steps.label: Explanation
old_steps.body:
Only people who are **willing to compromise** should undergo **mediation** to resolve their conflicts.

M → WC

Actual **litigation** should be pursued only when one is **sure** that one's position is **correct**.

L → SC

People whose **conflicts are based on ideology** are **unwilling to compromise**.

I → ~WC

old_notes.body: Falsely assumes that people who do not undergo mediation should pursue litigation.
No relationship can be established between people whose conflicts are not based on ideology and people who should pursue litigation.

There is a difference between “should be sure” and “are sure.”
Also, this assumes that those who should not undergo mediation are not always sure that their positions are correct.
Falsely assumes that people who are sure of the correctness of their position are not willing to compromise.
This follows from the first and third statements.

steps.label: Given
steps.body:
Although some nutritional facts about soft drinks are listed on their labels, exact caffeine content is not.
That's a fact about today: caffeine content isn't listed.

Listing exact caffeine content would make it easier to limit, but not eliminate, one's caffeine intake.
Listed → Easier to limit

If it became easier for people to limit, but not eliminate, their caffeine intake, many people would do so, which would improve their health.
Easier to limit → Many people limit → Their health improves

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Look for the shared term. "Easier to limit, but not eliminate" is the result of the second sentence and the trigger of the third. That lets us chain them:

Listed → Easier to limit → Many people limit → Their health improves

Now the first sentence. It's a fact, and it negates the start of the chain: caffeine content is not listed. A negated trigger tells us nothing, so the chain only describes what would happen if the content were listed. Any answer about what happens because it isn't listed is going past the statements.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Predict the chain from start to finish, kept hypothetical: if exact caffeine content were listed, some people's health would improve.

Watch for answers that run the chain from "not listed," and answers that swap limiting for eliminating.

notes.body:
This is the chain read end to end, in the same hypothetical mood as the stimulus. Listed → easier to limit → many people limit → their health improves. "Many people" guarantees "at least some people," so the weaker wording is safely proven.

Notice A says "would" and "if exact caffeine content were listed." It doesn't claim anyone's health is improving now, which matters because the first sentence tells us the content isn't listed. A good Must Be True answer keeps both the chain and its conditions.

B starts from the actual situation: content not listed. That negates the trigger of the second statement, and a negated trigger proves nothing. The stimulus says listing would make limiting easier. It never says people can't limit at all without it. B turns "easier" into "possible."

C also starts from content not being listed (people have to guess), and then switches from limiting to eliminating. The stimulus is explicit that listing would help people limit, "but not eliminate," their intake. It says nothing about how hard eliminating is when people have to guess.

The statements say listing caffeine content would make it easier to limit, "but not eliminate," one's caffeine intake. They say nothing about whether people who want to eliminate caffeine would benefit, so this does not have to be true.

The only health effect the stimulus describes is improvement for the many people who limit their intake. Could someone else's health get worse? Maybe, but nothing in the statements says so, and a Must Be True answer needs proof, not possibility.

old_steps.label: Given
old_steps.body:
Although some nutritional facts about soft drinks are listed on their labels, exact caffeine content is not.

Listing exact caffeine content would make it easier to limit, but not eliminate, one's caffeine intake.
LCC → ELC

If it became easier for people to limit, but not eliminate, their caffeine intake, many people would do so, which would improve their health.
ELC → IH

old_notes.body:
This follows from the second and third statements chained together.

LCC → ELC → IH

If exact caffeine content were listed, limiting would be easier, many people would limit their intake, and their health would improve. So at least some people's health would improve.

This negates the second statement.

~LCC → ~ELC

The stimulus says listing makes limiting easier. It doesn't say that without listing, people can't limit their intake at all, so B treats "easier" as if it meant "possible."

This negates the second statement, and it also switches from limiting to eliminating.

~LCC → ~ELC

The stimulus says listing would make it easier to limit, "but not eliminate," caffeine intake. It tells us nothing about how hard eliminating caffeine is when people have to guess.

The statements say listing caffeine content would make it easier to limit, "but not eliminate," one's caffeine intake. They say nothing about whether people who want to eliminate caffeine would benefit, so this does not have to be true.

This goes against the inference from the second and third statements.

LCC → ELC → IH

The only effect the stimulus describes from listing caffeine content is improved health. Nothing in it supports anyone's health getting worse, so E doesn't have to be true.

steps.label: Given
steps.body:
The profits of downtown businesses will increase if more consumers live in the downtown area.
↑C → ↑P

A decrease in the cost of living in the downtown area will guarantee that the number of consumers living there will increase.
↓CL → ↑C

However, the profits of downtown businesses will not increase unless downtown traffic congestion decreases.
↑P → ↓TC

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Three conditionals, and they overlap. More consumers is the result of the second and the trigger of the first. Higher profits is the result of the first and the trigger of the third ("not increase unless" puts lower congestion on the necessary side). Line them up:

↓CL → ↑C → ↑P → ↓TC

Read the chain like a one-way street. Anything on the left guarantees everything to its right. Nothing on the right guarantees anything to its left. Lower congestion is required for higher profits, but it doesn't produce them.

The contrapositive runs the other way with every term negated: if congestion doesn't fall, profits won't rise, the number of residents won't increase, and the cost of living won't decrease.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Every answer is a conditional, so the test is direction. A correct answer moves left to right along the chain, or right to left with both sides negated. Expect something like ↓CL → ↑P, ↑C → ↓TC, or ↓CL → ↓TC.

Any answer that starts at ↓TC and claims something follows is backwards.

notes.body: ↓TC → ↑C runs the chain backward. Lower congestion sits at the far right: it's what higher profits require. A requirement doesn't trigger anything. Congestion could fall while the cost of living and the number of residents stay exactly where they are. The valid version goes the other way: ↑C → ↓TC.

Start at the left end. A lower cost of living guarantees more consumers living downtown (second statement), and more consumers guarantees higher profits (first statement). Two links, so ↓CL → ↑P.

The move on a chain question: find the term that is the result of one rule and the trigger of another, connect them, then check each answer by asking whether its "if" sits to the left of its "then" on your chain.

C starts from the right end of the chain, which triggers nothing, and lands on an increase in the cost of living, which no rule even mentions. The statements only cover what follows a decrease in the cost of living. Nothing could prove the cost goes up.

D is the full chain read in reverse. The statements give ↓CL → ↓TC: if the cost of living falls, congestion must fall too. D flips it to ↓TC → ↓CL. Lower congestion is only a requirement for higher profits, so it can't send us back up the chain.

This is the most tempting trap because the two terms really are linked. Only the direction is wrong.

The first statement says more consumers → higher profits. E reverses it: higher profits → more consumers. Profits could rise for some other reason, like more shoppers commuting in, and the statements never say residents are the only way to raise profits.

old_steps.label: Given
old_steps.body:
The profits of downtown businesses will increase if more consumers live in the downtown area.
↑C → ↑P

A decrease in the cost of living in the downtown area will guarantee that the number of consumers living there will increase.
↓CL → ↑C

However, the profits of downtown businesses will not increase unless downtown traffic congestion decreases.
↑P → ↓TC

old_notes.body:
This reverses the inference that can be made from the first and third statements.
↑C → ↑P
↑P → ↓TC
∴ ↑C → ↓TC

This follows from the first and second statements.
↓CL → ↑C
↑C → ↑P
∴ ↓CL → ↑P

The statements tell us what follows when the cost of living decreases, not what follows when traffic congestion decreases. A decrease in congestion is only a necessary condition for higher profits, so it triggers nothing, and nothing in the statements says the cost of living will increase.
↓CL → ↑C → ↑P → ↓TC

This reverses the inference that can be made from all three statements.
↓CL → ↑C
↑C → ↑P
↑P → ↓TC
∴ ↓CL → ↓TC

This reverses the first statement.
↑P → ↑C

steps.label: Given
steps.body:
Claim 1: For several decades, the number of transistors on new microchips has doubled about every 18 months, "and hence" so has computing speed. Each doubling in transistors brought a doubling in speed.

Claim 2: From the mid-1990s into the next decade, each doubling in computing speed was accompanied by a doubling in the cost of producing the microchip.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
What do the two claims share? Doubling in computing speed. Claim 1 ties each transistor doubling to a speed doubling. Claim 2 ties each speed doubling, in that window, to a cost doubling. Connect them through the shared term:

Transistors double → speed doubles → (mid-1990s into next decade) cost doubles

Now notice the limits. The cost fact covers only the mid-1990s into the next decade. Nothing tells us why costs doubled, what happened to the retail price of computers, what engineers were trying to do, or whether the pattern will continue.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Predict the substitution, with its time window intact: from the mid-1990s into the next decade, each doubling in transistors came with a doubling in production cost.

Expect wrong answers to stretch past what was reported: the only way to raise speed, retail prices, engineers' motives, or the future.

notes.body: The statements do link the two: the number of transistors doubled, "and hence" computing speed doubled. But they never say adding transistors is the only effective way to double computing speed. The word "only" goes beyond what the statements support.
The statements are about the cost of producing microchips, not the retail cost of computers. Nothing tells us how retail prices changed, so B can't be inferred.
The statements say nothing about what engineers focused on or whether they tried to control costs. The cost doubling is reported as a fact, not as the result of anyone ignoring cost.

D substitutes one term for its partner. Claim 2 pairs each speed doubling with a cost doubling. Claim 1 says speed doubled because transistors doubled, so each transistor doubling is a speed doubling. Put transistors where speed was, and you get D. "Fabricating" is just another word for producing, and D keeps the mid-1990s window.

When two statements share a term, try substituting one into the other. On many Must Be True questions, that substitution is the whole inference.
The cost doubling is reported only for the mid-1990s into the next decade. A pattern from that period tells us nothing about whether engineers will ever break it.

old_steps.label: Given
old_steps.body: For several decades, the number of transistors on new computer microchips, and hence the microchips’ computing speed, has doubled about every 18 months. However, from the mid-1990s into the next decade, each such doubling in a microchip’s computing speed was accompanied by a doubling in the cost of producing that microchip.

old_notes.body: The statements do link the two: the number of transistors doubled, "and hence" computing speed doubled. But they never say adding transistors is the only effective way to double computing speed. The word "only" goes beyond what the statements support.
The statements are about the cost of producing microchips, not the retail cost of computers. Nothing tells us how retail prices changed, so B can't be inferred.
The statements say nothing about what engineers focused on or whether they tried to control costs. The cost doubling is reported as a fact, not as the result of anyone ignoring cost.
This restates the second premise.
The cost doubling is reported only for the mid-1990s into the next decade. A pattern from that period tells us nothing about whether engineers will ever break it.

steps.label: Given
steps.body:
The expert rejects a proposed test: "any substance that at least some habitual users can cease to use is nonaddictive." Used as the only criterion, that test would label some prime examples of addictive substances nonaddictive.

Then the expert gives a requirement that any adequate set of criteria must include. "Only if" introduces the necessary side:

Addictive → withdrawal causes most users extreme psychological and physiological difficulty

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The only conditional is the last sentence. Addictive substances have to be hard to quit for most users. Contrapositive: if withdrawal does not cause most users extreme difficulty, the substance is not addictive.

Now ask what the rejected test missed. A few users quitting tells us about some users. The requirement is about most users. Both can be true at once: a substance can be easy to quit for a handful and brutal for the majority. That's exactly how the prime examples of addictive substances slip past the some-users test.

Notice also what the rule can't do. It gives a requirement for addictiveness. It never says what is enough to make something addictive.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Expect an answer that applies the requirement in the right direction, probably playing some against most: a substance some users quit easily can still be addictive, but only if most users have a hard time.

Be ready to reject answers that treat the requirement as sufficient, or that talk about one person instead of most users.

notes.body: A reverses the rule. Extreme difficulty is required for addictiveness, not enough for it. A also shrinks "most users" to a single person. One person struggling to quit can't satisfy a requirement about most users, and even satisfying it wouldn't prove the substance is addictive.
The expert compares an adequate definition with a rejected proposal, not with present practice. We have no count of what is deemed addictive now, so we can't prove the number would shrink.

Let's unpack C. Its subject is a substance some users can quit easily. It says that substance is addictive only if most users can't quit easily:

Addictive → NOT (most users quit with little or no difficulty)

The expert's rule gives Addictive → most users have extreme difficulty. If most users have extreme difficulty, it can't be true that most quit with little or no difficulty. So C follows.

The "some users" opening is what makes C look hard, but it's only setup. A few easy quitters don't decide anything, because the rule cares about most. When an answer wraps a rule in extra conditions, strip it to its arrow and compare it with the stimulus's arrow.

D talks about one person who used a substance without difficulty. The rule is about withdrawal causing difficulty for most users. Easy use says nothing about quitting, and one person says nothing about most. To conclude nonaddictive, we'd need the requirement to fail for most users, and D never shows that.

The expert says what any adequate set of criteria must embody, which treats adequate criteria as possible. Disagreement over one proposed test doesn't show the term can't be defined precisely. Nothing supports "impossible."

old_steps.label: Given
old_steps.body: Some have suggested that any substance that at least some habitual users can cease to use is nonaddictive. However, if this is taken to be the sole criterion of nonaddictiveness, some substances that most medical experts classify as prime examples of addictive substances would be properly deemed nonaddictive. A substance is addictive only if withdrawal from its habitual use causes most users extreme psychological and physiological difficulty.

old_notes.body: This reverses the third statement. WCD → A
The statements do not indicate how many substances are deemed to be addictive at present.
This rephrases the third statement. A → WCD
The issue is not substance use, but rather the withdrawal from the use of that substance.
That there is a disagreement about the definition of the term “addiction” does not mean that it is impossible to define with precision.

steps.label: Given
steps.body:
Three rules from the style manual.

1. Older works: archaic spelling or punctuation that occurs infrequently and does not interfere with comprehension → preserve it.
2. Older works: archaic spelling or punctuation that occurs frequently → the editor may modernize it, with an explanatory note in the text, or, if similar modernizing was done in more than one quotation, a general statement in the preface.
3. Modern works: obvious typographical error → may be corrected without explanation.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Watch the modal words. Rule 1 says "are to be preserved": a requirement. Rule 2 says "may": permission, not a duty. Rule 3 also says "may." An answer that turns a "may" into a "should" goes beyond the manual.

Then watch the triggers. Rule 2 needs only one thing: archaic material from an older work that occurs frequently. Whether it interferes doesn't matter. Rule 3 covers obvious typos in modern works, not archaic spellings. And the manual is silent about some cases, like an archaic form that occurs infrequently but does interfere. Neither rule 1 nor rule 2 triggers there, so nothing follows.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer that triggers a rule cleanly and keeps its strength. The likeliest shape: archaic spelling or punctuation from an older work that occurs frequently may be modernized. Extra details are fine as long as the whole trigger is there.

notes.body: A never says the word comes from an older work. If the correction fixes an obvious typo in a quotation from a modern work, rule 3 lets the editor correct it without explanation. And even in an older work, a word that occurs only once isn't frequent, so rule 2, the only rule that calls for supplying an explanation, never triggers.

Rule 3 is the only rule about modern works, and it covers obvious typographical errors, not archaic spellings. Rules 1 and 2 cover older works only. Nothing in the manual permits modernizing an archaic spelling in a modern work, with or without an explanation.

The style manual never says an editor should modernize anything. Rule 2 gives permission ("may") when archaic forms occur frequently. Interference with comprehension only tells us rule 1's preserve requirement doesn't apply. Escaping a duty to preserve isn't the same as gaining a duty to modernize.

D gives us punctuation quoted from an older work that occurs frequently. That's the full trigger for rule 2, so the editor may modernize it. The extra detail, that it interferes with comprehension, doesn't hurt: a rule still applies when you know more than its trigger. And D keeps the manual's "may" instead of upgrading it to "should."

On rule-application questions, check two things: is the whole trigger present, and does the answer keep the rule's strength?

Rule 2 allows a general statement in the preface when similar modernizing has been done in more than one quotation. E describes modernizing only one instance, so the preface option isn't triggered. E also turns the manual's options into a "should": the manual says where an explanation can go, not that it must go in the preface.

old_steps.label: Given
old_steps.body: Archaic spellings and styles of punctuation in direct quotations from older works are to be preserved if they occur infrequently and do not interfere with a reader’s comprehension. However, if they occur frequently, the editor may modernize them, inserting a note with an explanation to this effect in the text, or if similar modernizing has been done in more than one quotation, inserting a general statement in the preface. On the other hand, obvious typographical errors in quotations from modern works may be corrected without explanation.

old_notes.body: This answer never says the quoted word comes from an older work. If the correction fixes an obvious typographical error in a quotation from a modern work, the third statement says it may be corrected without explanation, so an explanation is not required.
From the first and second statements the editor should preserve the archaic spelling of a quoted word or provide an explanation if it is modernized.

The style manual never says an editor should modernize anything. Archaic spellings may be modernized if they occur frequently, and are to be preserved if they occur infrequently and do not interfere with comprehension. Knowing that a spelling interferes only tells us the preservation rule does not apply; it does not create a duty to modernize.
~F + ~IRC → P

This answer provides more than enough information to trigger the second statement.
F + IRC → MM

The second part of the second statement implies that if such modernizing has been done in more than one quotation, a statement in the preface should be included. But to say that is true if such modernizing has been done in only one of several similar instances goes beyond what can be inferred.
